linkedin.activityText: Arianna Huffington Arianna Huffington 19h Arianna Huffington shared this Most of us already know what supports better health, but the challenge is making those behaviors part of daily life. And today Thrive Global and Deloitte are launching a strategic relationship that makes it easier for people to move from awareness to action so they can build healthier habits and improve their health — one Microstep at a time. Currently, most U.S. healthcare spending is reactive, focused on treating illnesses and conditions after they occur. But Deloitte estimates that proactive “well-care” could save the country up to $2.2 trillion a year in medical and pharmacy costs. This number captures the enormous opportunity we have to move the needle. By bringing together Thrive’s AI-powered behavior change platform and Deloitte’s experience in health care transformation, data and analytics, digital innovation and large-scale implementation, we’ll help organizations harness the science-backed power of our daily behaviors — food, movement, sleep, stress management and connection — and scale behavior change to help people build healthier habits and routines. And starting in October, Deloitte will incorporate Thrive content across key areas of health into the wellbeing resources available to its U.S. workforce. Learn more about how Thrive Global and Deloitte are helping organizations support health and wellbeing through behavior change here: https://lnkd.in/dEBtA3Sw Arianna Huffington reacted on this Arianna Huffington reacted on this Melinda French Gates Melinda French Gates 1d Arianna Huffington reacted on this Have you ever felt like the price of your professional success is your own health and well-being? If so, you’re not alone. This collective delusion has told so many women that if we want to advance at work, we have to sleep less, push through exhaustion, ignore pain, and put ourselves last. When we neglect our health, everything else becomes harder. Running on empty may help us power through in the moment, but over time it can lead to burnout, chronic health challenges, and consequences that outlast any job or promotion. Is this really what success looks like? Changing this requires more than an individual mindset shift. Women deserve—and we all benefit from—health systems and workplaces that make it easier for people to get the care they need and pursue their ambitions at the same time. The goal shouldn't be helping women choose between their health and their dreams. It should be making sure they never have to. What a beautiful story of hope in The @Guardian. Twenty-one years ago, a field in Norfolk was home to a single crop. Today, it is a wildflower meadow with more than 150 plant species. Since 2011, the only maintenance has been one hay cut each summer. The cut keeps the field from becoming woodland and gives more delicate wildflowers room to grow.

As @UCL Professor Carl Sayer put it: “Sometimes we’re not patient enough.” And after watching the meadow become more biodiverse each year, he says, “It’s hope — we can recover things. We just need to do less in the recovery process.”

Life is a dance between making it happen and letting it happen. In this meadow, making it happen means one simple act of care each year. Letting it happen means trusting nature and giving it time. The same is true in our lives: our daily choices around sleep, food, movement, stress and connection give our bodies and minds the support they need to renew.

Read more in The Guardian at the link in bio.

Congratulations @ArielEmanuel on the publication of Roll the Calls!

Of course I knew Ari had an amazing story. Angry boy from Chicago overcomes severe dyslexia, rises from mailroom to C-suite, transforms himself into one of the legendary dealmakers and visionaries in Hollywood history – I expected Ari’s memoir to be a page-turner. But I didn’t expect such tenderness, such sweetness, so much heart. I wasn’t ready for all the wisdom about mental health and self-confidence and resilience and the search for one’s true happiness. I simply wasn’t prepared for Shoe Dog meets Goodfellas with a dash of The Little Prince. What a pleasant, refreshing, and wonderful surprise this book is.

And that’s my blurb for the book! You can get a copy at the link in bio.

Looking back at two great days at @Dreamforce. @Salesforce’s chief marketing officer @ErinOles moderated a conversation with @officiallymcconaughey and me about who shapes culture in the age of AI.

Here’s what nobody wants to admit about the content explosion: the bottleneck was never production. It was always judgment. For most of history, we assumed the hard part was making things — and the machines have now solved that. Anyone can generate a screenplay, a song, a strategy deck in seconds. But Matthew put his finger on what the machines haven’t solved: AI can tell you what’s popular, but it doesn’t yet have an ear for what’s really good.

Those are profoundly different things. Popularity is a pattern in the data. Good is a judgment — and judgment is built from everything that never shows up in training data: taste formed over decades, failures metabolized into instinct, the thousand small refinements of a lived life. Erin compressed it into one line: the real AI superpower isn’t the tool, it’s the taste.

Which means we’ve been worried about the wrong scarcity. The scarce resource of this era isn’t intelligence — machines have made intelligence abundant. It’s wisdom. And here’s the inconvenient truth about wisdom: it can’t be generated, downloaded, or scaled. It has to be lived into existence, one experience at a time.

Machines gather knowledge exponentially. Humans gather wisdom slowly. Whether that gap becomes a crisis or a renaissance depends entirely on whether we treat our own development as seriously as we treat the technology’s. And keeping people at the center of the AI conversation was the focus of my session at Dreamforce with chief people officer Nathalie Scardino and HR leaders from around the world.

A beautiful evening celebrating the opening of the @LucasMuseum of Narrative Art — a museum as expansive, surprising and impossible to categorize as the works it celebrates.

The museum houses the art collection of George Lucas and @MellodyHobson. At a time when AI dominates our public conversation, it’s a reminder that machines aren’t the only ones producing wonders. It’s a cathedral of wonder and awe, human creativity, storytelling and connection. As Mellody said, “Narrative art creates an emotional connection, not an intellectual one.”

The museum looks, appropriately, like a spaceship, rising, curving and folding into the landscape – in fact, there isn’t a right angle anywhere in the building. Works associated with empires and religious traditions live alongside illustrations, comic strips and movie images that have shaped our lives. There is even an immersive reproduction of the Sistine Chapel ceiling, which George calls “God’s comic book” because its panels tell a story. And throughout, cinema is treated not as something separate from art history but as another chapter in our ancient drive to turn experience into narrative. It’s why one of the museum’s theaters is named for Robert Flaherty, a pioneer of documentary filmmaking.

And then there are the monsters. The museum’s exploration of them brought to mind what Guillermo del Toro’s work shows about monsters being revealing mirrors. We create them to give form to what frightens us and to explore the parts of ourselves we can’t always confront directly. The same is true of the myths, which let us wrestle with the same big questions at a larger scale. The characters and settings change but the elemental questions remain: Who are we? What do we fear? What are we willing to fight for? And who can we become?

At a moment when so much is pulling us apart, George Lucas and Mellody Hobson have created a home for the images, stories and myths that unite us — a place where art is an invitation to feel, wonder and see ourselves in one another.

As we mark World Alzheimer’s Day, more than 7 million people over age 65 in the US are living with Alzheimer’s disease — a figure that is projected to almost double in the next few decades. And more than 12 million people are caregivers to loved ones with Alzheimer’s or other dementias. There’s no sugarcoating a disease that results in the widespread loss of brain function, and no number that captures the heartbreak of seeing a loved one decline. And yet, there is reason for hope.

That’s because research shows that Alzheimer’s-related brain changes can begin up to 20 years before symptoms set in, highlighting the importance of investing in our brain health and addressing modifiable risk factors throughout adulthood.

This is a 20-year window of opportunity. As with so many chronic conditions, research is showing that with brain health, our DNA is not necessarily our destiny. We have more power than we previously thought to shape our brain health, both day-to-day and in the long run.

Read more in @incmagazine at the link in bio.

Thursday evening on brain health was the largest event I’ve ever had in my home. And it so perfectly captured the sense of possibility of this moment, when brain health has moved from medical journals to the center of the conversation on health. I moderated a wide-ranging conversation with Andrew Adams, Group VP of Molecule Discovery, Lilly Research Laboratories, who shared not only about his work on molecular discovery and genetic medicines, but how it is inspired by the lived experience of his mother and grandmother; Konstantina Stankovic, the chair of otolaryngology and head and neck surgery at @Stanford Medicine, who urged us to “protect our senses,” since our hearing, smell and other senses are key inputs to the brain and some of the first signals that can tell us when an intervention is needed; and Baba Shiv, a behavioral neuroscientist and professor at the @StanfordGSB, who shared that when multitasking and distraction are taking such a toll on our brain health, one of the best Microsteps we can take is to “learn how to subtract before you can add.”

It was a great conversation, and one of the themes that emerged was that with brain health, the biggest innovations are being driven not by competitive advantage but “collaborative advantage.”

And the collective wisdom in the room proved it. As we opened the floor to questions and comments, we heard from authors (neurologist @teenashettymd, whose Healing the Brain came out earlier this month, and Sandro Galea, Dean at the School of Public Health at Washington University in St. Louis and author most recently of Why Health?), entrepreneurs (Shiv Rao, CEO and co-founder of AI health company Abridge), and clinicians including Dr. David Dodick, Chief Medical Officer at the Atria Health and Research Institute, and Brendan G. Carr, the CEO of Mount Sinai Health System.

New research from @gallup and @pivotaldotcom quantifies what women have been reporting for years: women face significant barriers in getting healthcare, and these barriers affect more than just health outcomes.

51% of women report at least one negative experience with healthcare providers — symptoms dismissed, misdiagnosis, or not getting needed answers. For men, it’s 39%.

The findings also make clear that the consequences extend well beyond health outcomes. 54% of women report an impact on family life or relationships, 42% on work or career, and 32% on community participation.
That’s the reframe this research offers: barriers to care are not only a health problem. They’re a barrier to opportunity, with effects that ripple through families, workplaces, communities, and our economy.

Women are accomplishing so much despite these barriers. Imagine the possibilities — for their health, their connections, and so much more — if they got the care they needed.

Read more at the link in bio.

Yesterday afternoon at @Dreamforce with @Salesforce President and Chief People Officer Nathalie Scardino and a group of people leaders talking about AI, work, and what it means to be irreplaceably human.

AI is now saving managers nearly three hours per week. But 36% of them say they waste more than half of it.

It’s called the AI Efficiency Trap — when productivity gains create pressure to simply do more, feeding the very stress and burnout the technology was supposed to relieve. 

Avoiding that trap is the real opportunity for leaders — and it’s much bigger than deploying new tools. It’s being intentional about the time AI gives back: reinvesting it in recharging, in creativity, in connection, in the work that requires our full attention and judgment. And it’s making clear to your people that their value is measured not in additional output for its own sake, but in their capacity to think, create and connect.

The companies that thrive in this era won’t be defined by how much time AI saved them, but by how deliberately they reinvested it.

Got questions about brain health? Join Arianna Huffington, Dr. Vin Gupta, and Dr. Brandy Matthews, for an AMA in r/science on World Alzheimer’s Day, 9/21! Link in bio.

Love this poem from @officiallymcconaughey’s “Poems & Prayers” that’s now on my nightstand. Looking forward to my conversation with Matthew and @Salesforce CMO Erin Oles tomorrow at @Dreamforce.

We talk a lot about how to succeed in a job we love. But how we navigate a job we don’t love matters too. As I shared with the @WSJ, “You approach staying in a job you don’t love very differently if you don’t operate from a place of fear and despair.”

Our wellbeing is not just about helping us thrive when things are going well. It gives us the resilience and perspective to see new possibilities and make decisions from a place of strength.

Read more in Allison Pohle’s article, “The 24 New Rules for Succeeding at Work” in The Wall Street Journal.

analysis.summary: Arianna Huffington is the founder and CEO of Thrive Global, a behavior change technology company focused on improving health outcomes and productivity. She is also the founder of The Huffington Post. Her work centers on the intersection of technology, well-being, and human potential, advocating for a shift from reactive healthcare to proactive 'well-care' and emphasizing the importance of sleep, stress management, and connection. She is a prolific writer and speaker, actively engaging with topics like AI, brain health, and the balance between ambition and personal well-being. Her public persona is one of an influential thought leader who values family, wisdom, and making a positive societal impact.
